title: Maxwell's Thermodynamic Relations
short_intro: Maxwell's thermodynamic relations are fundamental equality statements involving partial derivatives of thermodynamic state variables. They are derived from exact differentials of thermodynamic potentials.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Direct application of the four primary Maxwell relations, cyclic rule, and simple partial differentiation in PVT systems.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Derivation of Maxwell relations from state functions, Tds equations, energy equations, and application to specific heat relations and Joule-Thomson effect.

prerequisites: Concept of Temperature and internal energy
First and Second Laws of Thermodynamics

concept_notes.heading: Foundation of Maxwell Relations
bullets: Thermodynamic potentials (Internal Energy U, Helmholtz Free Energy F, Enthalpy H, Gibbs Free Energy G) are state functions with exact differentials.
For any exact differential dz = M dx + N dy, the condition for exactness is (dM/dy)_x = (dN/dx)_y.
Applying this mathematical theorem to the four thermodynamic potentials yields the four primary Maxwell relations.

concept_notes.heading: First Maxwell Relation (from Internal Energy U)
bullets: Internal energy is expressed as dU = T dS - P dV.
The relation is obtained by equating the cross derivatives of temperature and pressure with respect to volume and entropy.
Equation: (dT/dV)_S = - (dP/dS)_V, linking thermal and mechanical variables adiabatically.

concept_notes.heading: Second and Third Maxwell Relations (Helmholtz F and Enthalpy H)
bullets: Helmholtz free energy function F = U - TS gives dF = - S dT - P dV, leading to (dS/dV)_T = (dP/dT)_V.
Enthalpy function H = U + PV gives dH = T dS + V dP, leading to (dT/dP)_S = (dV/dS)_P.
These relations are extensively used to evaluate changes in entropy using measurable quantities like volume expansion coefficient.

concept_notes.heading: Fourth Maxwell Relation (from Gibbs Free Energy G)
bullets: Gibbs free energy function G = H - TS gives dG = - S dT + V dP.
This relation is crucial in understanding the effect of pressure on phase transitions and melting points.

derivations.title: Derivation of First Maxwell Relation from Internal Energy
derivations.conditions: Single-phase, closed system in thermal and mechanical equilibrium
steps: Write the combined First and Second Law of Thermodynamics: dU = T dS - P dV.
Treat U as a function of S and V, so that dU = (partial U/partial S)_V dS + (partial U/partial V)_S dV.
Identify coefficients: T = (partial U/partial S)_V and -P = (partial U/partial V)_S.
Since dU is an exact differential, apply Euler's reciprocity condition: partial / partial V (partial U/partial S)_V = partial / partial S (partial U/partial V)_S.
Substitute the coefficients to obtain (partial T/partial V)_S = - (partial P/partial S)_V.

derivations.title: Derivation of Fourth Maxwell Relation from Gibbs Free Energy
steps: Define Gibbs free energy as G = H - TS = U + PV - TS.
Differentiate G: dG = dU + P dV + V dP - T dS - S dT.
Substitute dU = T dS - P dV into the equation, yielding dG = -S dT + V dP.
Treat G as a function of T and P: dG = (\partial G/\partial T)_P dT + (\partial G/\partial P)_T dP.
Apply the exactness condition to mixed partial derivatives: \partial / \partial P (\partial G/\partial T)_P = \partial / \partial T (\partial G/\partial P)_T.
Equate terms to arrive at -(\partial S/\partial P)_T = (\partial V/\partial T)_P.

formula_sheet.name: First TdS Equation
formula_sheet.equation_html: T dS = C_V dT + T \left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial T}\right)_V dV
formula_sheet.variables: C_V = Heat capacity at constant volume

formula_sheet.name: Second TdS Equation
formula_sheet.equation_html: T dS = C_P dT - T \left(/left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_P dP
formula_sheet.variables: C_P = Heat capacity at constant pressure

formula_sheet.name: Energy Equation for Internal Energy
formula_sheet.equation_html: \left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial V}\right)_T = T \left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial T}\right)_V - P

formula_sheet.name: Difference in Heat Capacities
formula_sheet.equation_html: C_P - C_V = T \left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial T}\right)_V \left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_P

solved_numericals.question: Using the cyclic relation for thermodynamic variables P, V, and T, show that \left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial V}\right)_T \left(/left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_P \left(\frac{\partial T}{\partial P}\right)_V = -1.
solution_steps: Let a function f(P, V, T) = 0 define the state of a system.
Write the total differential of P as a function of V and T: dP = (\partial P/\partial V)_T dV + (\partial P/\partial T)_V dT.
Set dP = 0 for an isothermal process or substitute dT from dT = (\partial T/\partial P)_V dP + (\partial T/\partial V)_P dV.
Rearrange terms to obtain the standard cyclic chain rule identity: (\partial P/\partial V)_T (\partial V/\partial T)_P (\partial T/\partial P)_V = -1.
solved_numericals.answer: Proven analytically using partial derivative identities.

solved_numericals.question: For a van der Waals gas with equation of state (P + a/V^2)(V - b) = RT, find the internal energy expression (\partial U/\partial V)_T using Maxwell thermodynamic relations.
solution_steps: Use the energy equation derived from Maxwell relations: (\partial U/\partial V)_T = T (\partial P/\partial T)_V - P.
From the van der Waals equation, express P as a function of T and V: P = \frac{RT}{V-b} - \frac{a}{V^2}.
Differentiate P with respect to T at constant V: (\partial P/\partial T)_V = \frac{R}{V-b}.
Substitute into the energy equation: (\partial U/\partial V)_T = T \left(\frac{R}{V-b}\right) - \left(\frac{RT}{V-b} - \frac{a}{V^2}\right).
Simplify the expression to get a/V^2.

solved_numericals.question: Prove that for any substance, C_P - C_V = V \beta^2 T / \kappa_T, where \beta is the volume expansivity and \kappa_T is the isothermal compressibility.
solution_steps: Start with the general relation C_P - C_V = T (\partial P/\partial T)_V (\partial V/\partial T)_P.
Define volume expansivity \beta = \frac{1}{V} (\partial V/\partial T)_P, so (\partial V/\partial T)_P = V \beta.
Using the cyclic rule, (\partial P/\partial T)_V = - (\partial P/\partial V)_T (\partial V/\partial T)_P = \frac{V \beta}{V \kappa_T} = \frac{\beta}{\kappa_T}.
Substitute back into the difference equation to obtain C_P - C_V = T (\beta / \kappa_T) (V \beta) = \frac{V \beta^2 T}{\kappa_T}.

assumptions_and_limitations: Applicable only to systems in thermodynamic equilibrium where state functions and exact differentials are well-defined.
Do not apply directly to irreversible or non-equilibrium processes unless evaluated across equilibrium states.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Maxwell relations are only valid for ideal gases.
common_misconceptions.correct: Maxwell relations are universal and apply to any pure substance in equilibrium, whether solid, liquid, or gas, ideal or real.
common_misconceptions.why: They originate purely from the mathematical property of exact differentials of state functions, independent of the equation of state.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The minus signs in Maxwell relations are arbitrary.
common_misconceptions.correct: The negative signs are mathematically mandatory and arise directly from the cross-differentiation of potentials like U and G.
common_misconceptions.why: Swapping independent variables in differentials introduces negative signs through the cyclic rule and properties of partial derivatives.

quick_revision: The four potentials U, F, H, G generate the four Maxwell relations via exact differentials: dU (T,-P), dF (-S,-P), dH (T,V), dG (-S,V).
First Maxwell Relation: \left(\frac{\partial T}{\partial V}\right)_S = -\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial S}\right)_V
Second Maxwell Relation: \left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial V}\right)_T = \left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial T}\right)_V
